title: A full-wave method-of-moments solver for automated antenna design
desc: Implementation and analytical validation of an RWG and EFIE boundary-element solver integrated with iterative optimization, full-wave verification and surrogate calibration for implantable and wearable antennas.
heroCaption: Conforming surface mesh and resonant surface-current distribution for a meandered inverted-F antenna.
body:
Full-wave electromagnetic simulation / 20 verification tests / Python, NumPy, SciPy and Gmsh / approximately 3,000 lines / source code

Automated optimization of implantable and wearable antennas requires a full-wave validation layer capable of identifying candidate designs that satisfy surrogate objectives while violating Maxwell-consistent electromagnetic behaviour. We developed an electric-field integral-equation solver with Rao-Wilton-Glisson basis functions, validated its numerical implementation against analytical scattering and antenna solutions, isolated three sources of apparently physical but numerically spurious resonances and incorporated the solver into an iterative optimization, verification and calibration framework.

1. Motivation and design requirements

The antenna-design pipeline combines a language-model controller with parametric templates for meandered inverted-F antennas, planar inverted-F antennas, loops and patches, together with CMA-ES and Bayesian optimization, matching-network synthesis and specific absorption rate calculations. Its original objective functions depended on closed-form estimates of resonance and input impedance, including effective-permittivity corrections, height-dependent radiation resistance and parallel-RLC approximations, while the OpenEMS and NEC2 interfaces reverted to the same analytical models rather than performing full-wave simulation.

Closed-form resonance estimates with expected errors of 20 to 30 percent are appropriate for initialization but insufficient for final design verification, particularly when geometric perturbations alter current paths in ways that violate the assumptions of the surrogate model. The required solver therefore had to evaluate the pipeline's native geometries within seconds on a laptop, avoid dependence on an external electromagnetic package and report the physical approximations retained by each simulation.

2. Boundary-element formulation

The target structures consist primarily of planar copper traces, conducting plates and narrow feed or shorting pins, for which a surface integral formulation avoids volumetric discretization while incorporating the radiation condition through the Green function. Although the resulting impedance matrix is dense, antenna meshes containing several hundred to several thousand unknowns remain compatible with direct LU factorization on a workstation.

The formulation is the electric-field integral equation (EFIE) with Rao–Wilton–Glisson (RWG) basis functions on a triangular mesh. On a perfect conductor the tangential electric field vanishes, so the scattered field produced by the unknown surface current \(\mathbf J\) must cancel the tangential impressed field,

\[ \hat n \times \Big[\, j\omega\mu_0 \!\int_S \mathbf J(\mathbf r')\,G\,dS' \,-\, \frac{1}{j\omega\varepsilon_0}\nabla\!\int_S \nabla'\!\cdot\mathbf J(\mathbf r')\,G\,dS' \Big] = \hat n \times \mathbf E^{\,i}(\mathbf r), \qquad G=\frac{e^{-jkR}}{4\pi R}. \]

Expanding \(\mathbf J=\sum_n I_n \mathbf f_n\) in RWG functions (each lives on a pair of triangles sharing an edge and carries unit current across that edge) and testing with the same functions gives the dense linear system \(\mathbf Z\mathbf I=\mathbf V\) with

\[ Z_{mn}= jk\eta\left[\iint \mathbf f_m\!\cdot\!\mathbf f_n\,G\,dS'dS \,-\, \frac{1}{k^2}\iint (\nabla\!\cdot\!\mathbf f_m)(\nabla'\!\cdot\!\mathbf f_n)\,G\,dS'dS\right]. \]

Accurate evaluation of the double surface integrals determines the numerical stability of the formulation because the Green-function kernel is singular for coincident triangles, nearly singular for adjacent elements and smooth but oscillatory at greater separation. Inadequate treatment of these regimes produces structured spurious resonances that can be difficult to distinguish from genuine antenna modes.

3. Computational architecture

The solver is organized into seven modules comprising approximately 1,200 lines that connect parametric geometry, conforming mesh generation, RWG basis construction, EFIE assembly, excitation and electromagnetic post-processing.

ModuleFunctionNumerical implementation
layout.pyAntennaGeometry → flat conductor panels + delta-gap linesPlanar trace segments are assembled into mitred ribbon polygons, conductor boxes are reduced to the electromagnetically relevant face, vertical pins inherit the transverse direction of the connected trace and ports are represented by gap lines with bridging ribbons where required. Coordinate snapping prevents copper-thickness dimensions from generating sliver faces.
gmsh_mesher.pyconforming triangulationOpenCASCADE fragment of every panel and line together, per-panel size fields with distance-based grading, structured (transfinite) meshes on ribbons, a triangle-quality gate with multi-algorithm retry.
mesh.pySurfaceMesh, RWG connectivityan edge shared by k ≥ 3 triangles (a pin meeting a plate) gets k−1 basis functions paired with the first triangle, which preserves Kirchhoff continuity at the junction without special junction bases.
quadrature.py · analytic.pyDunavant rules, closed-form \(\int_T dS'/R\) and \(\int_T \mathbf r' dS'/R\)the singular integrals are done exactly as sums over the three edges of the source triangle.
efie.pymatrix fillsparse basis matrices around a dense kernel, static part computed once per mesh, only the smooth remainder refilled per frequency.
excitation.py · postprocess.pyports, plane waves, far field, RCS, conductor lossstrip delta gap, \(V_m = V_0 l_m\) on every RWG edge crossing the gap line, \(Z_{in}=V_0/\sum I_m l_m\).
solver.pyMoMSolver with the analytical-solver interfaceFrequency sweeps, admittance-to-scattering conversion for multi-port structures and numerical diagnostics including power balance, electrical mesh size and omitted physical effects.

4. Numerical implementation

4.1 Quadrature and the singular integrals

Triangle integration uses symmetric Dunavant quadrature rules with 1, 3, 6 and 7 barycentric points and polynomial exactness through degrees 1, 2, 4 and 5. Evaluation against analytical integrals of barycentric monomials through the corresponding degree produced agreement to approximately 10-15.

Direct quadrature of the static kernel fails when an observation point lies on or near the source triangle, motivating decomposition of the Green function into a singular static term and a smooth frequency-dependent remainder. The remainder has a finite limit as the separation approaches zero and is evaluated numerically, whereas the static contribution is integrated analytically over the triangle edges.

\[ \int_T \frac{dS'}{R} = \sum_{i=1}^{3}\left[ P^0_i \ln\frac{R^+_i+l^+_i}{R^-_i+l^-_i} \,-\, |d|\left(\tan^{-1}\frac{P^0_i l^+_i}{(R^0_i)^2+|d|R^+_i} - \tan^{-1}\frac{P^0_i l^-_i}{(R^0_i)^2+|d|R^-_i}\right)\right], \]

A companion expression supplies the vector integral required by the RWG formulation, with the logarithmic form selected according to the position of the projected observation point to avoid indeterminate evaluation along an edge extension. Comparison with adaptive double integration at five in-plane and off-plane observation points showed agreement to eight decimal places and remained finite in the singular configurations where direct numerical integration failed.

4.2 Assembling Z without loops

Assembly was expressed as sparse basis operators surrounding a dense quadrature kernel, replacing explicit loops over test triangles, source triangles and quadrature coordinates. For a sparse basis matrix \(F_c\) containing weighted Cartesian RWG components and a divergence matrix \(D\), the vector and scalar potential contributions are obtained by sparse-dense matrix products.

\[ \mathbf A=\sum_{c\in\{x,y,z\}} F_c^{\mathsf T}\,\mathbb G\,F_c,\qquad \boldsymbol\Phi = D^{\mathsf T}\,\mathbb G\, D,\qquad \mathbf Z = jk\eta\left(\mathbf A - \boldsymbol\Phi/k^2\right), \]

The kernel matrix is evaluated in row blocks and is not retained in full, while near interactions replace the static contribution with analytical basis-level integrals and subdivide the outer test triangle when element sizes differ substantially. Frequency-independent static, analytical and conductor-loss matrices are cached for each mesh, leaving only the smooth remainder to be sampled with a three-point rule at each frequency and permitting a 21-frequency sweep of an 800-unknown antenna in approximately two seconds.

Conductor loss is represented by a Leontovich surface impedance \(Z_s=(1+j)\sqrt{\omega\mu_0/2\sigma}\), halved to account for current on both faces of a conducting sheet and incorporated through the RWG Gram matrix. Complex-valued \(k\) and \(\eta\) further permit homogeneous lossy media, including muscle-equivalent tissue at 400 MHz with relative permittivity 57 and conductivity 0.8 S/m, without modification of the assembly procedure.

4.3 Ports and post-processing

Excitation is represented by a strip delta gap that assigns \(V_m=\pm V_0l_m\) to each RWG edge crossing the port, with orientation selected to produce a consistent terminal current. Sequential excitation of each port yields the admittance, impedance and scattering matrices, while integration of the radiation vector over a 37 by 73 angular grid supplies radiated power and enables direct verification of power conservation against the complex input power.

5. Validation against analytical solutions

Numerical validation preceded application to parametric antenna templates and included canonical configurations that independently test port excitation, impedance assembly, surface-current continuity, radiation patterns, reciprocity and power conservation.

5.1 The half-wave strip dipole

5.2 Scattering from a sphere, against the Mie series

Because dipole validation jointly tests the excitation and impedance operators, matrix assembly was evaluated independently using plane-wave scattering from a perfectly conducting sphere. Monostatic radar cross-section agreed with the exact Mie-series solution within 0.35 dB across \(ka=0.6\) to 3 on a wavelength-over-ten mesh containing 1,068 unknowns, including the oscillatory resonance region.

5.3 Small loops against the textbook inductance

5.4 Reciprocity and energy

Automated verification further requires reciprocity within 10-3 for a two-port dipole pair separated by one sixth of a wavelength and power closure within 1 percent for a lossy copper dipole. These invariants provide sensitive tests for sign errors and normalization factors in the assembled operator.

6. Conforming meshes from parametric antenna geometries

Parametric templates represent conductors as finite-width traces, planar boxes and port definitions, which must be converted into mutually conforming surface panels before RWG connectivity can preserve current across trace intersections, plate boundaries and vertical junctions.

Mesh-convergence experiments established one transverse element for strips narrower than one fortieth of a wavelength and two elements for wider strips, plate elements no larger than one tenth of a wavelength or twice the nearest parallel-conductor spacing and gradual propagation of local refinement into adjacent panels. Junctions shared by \(k\) triangles use \(k-1\) RWG functions, which permits vertical pins to connect at arbitrary locations on a plate while preserving current continuity.

7. Numerical failure modes and correction

Application to the complete templates revealed narrow resonances at 525, 540, 570 and 640 MHz in the meandered inverted-F antenna and frequency-to-frequency impedance changes from 11 to 219 ohms in the planar inverted-F antenna, despite successful canonical validation. Controlled comparisons traced these apparently physical responses to matrix asymmetry, geometric end-cap extension and nonconforming CAD intersections.

7.1 Matrix asymmetry under symmetric factorization

Although the Galerkin EFIE operator is reciprocal and symmetric in exact arithmetic, numerical evaluation of near interactions produced relative asymmetry of approximately 10-3 because the two integration orders were not identical. Symmetric LDLT factorization silently discarded one triangle of this numerically asymmetric matrix, which amplified the discrepancy on graded meshes with condition numbers near 107 and generated spurious near-null modes.

Factorization of an identical impedance matrix by the two solvers isolated the failure, after which six-point and seven-point static quadrature rules produced a 700-ohm discrepancy under LDLT but only a 0.004-ohm discrepancy under LU. Explicit projection onto the reciprocal operator through \(\mathbf Z\leftarrow(\mathbf Z+\mathbf Z^{\mathsf T})/2\) followed by full LU factorization removed the spurious resonances.

7.2 Geometric bias from ribbon end caps

Ribbon construction initially added square end caps with half the trace width to ensure geometric overlap between connected segments. Although negligible for a 0.5-mm meander trace, this operation lengthened the 10-mm-wide validation dipole by 7 percent and shifted its resonance from 0.465 to 0.433 wavelengths, which was corrected by terminating ribbons flush and sharing the terminal edge with attached pins.

7.3 Nonconforming intersections between touching surfaces

Electrical continuity between a vertical pin and a conducting plate requires shared mesh edges, yet OpenCASCADE boolean fragmentation did not reliably imprint a face that only touched the interior of another face along an edge. The resulting geometry appeared connected in three-dimensional visualization while remaining electrically disconnected in the RWG graph.

Explicit embedding of pin boundaries connected the surfaces but duplicated geometric constraints and produced cascades of near-zero-area triangles under refinement. The final construction fragments pin endpoints into the host polygon, removes redundant embedding, applies structured transfinite meshing to ribbons, merges nodes within 10-3 element lengths and rejects meshes with minimum quality below 0.08 before retrying with an alternative algorithm, yielding stable meshes for all seven templates from refinement factors of 1.0 to 0.5.

7.4 Mesh-convergence analysis

8. Computational performance

9. Integration with multilevel optimization

The computational cost of full-wave evaluation precludes its use in every objective-function call, so the solver surrounds the analytical optimizer as a higher-fidelity verification and calibration stage.

  1. Verification. verify_design evaluates identical geometry with the analytical and full-wave models and reports resonance, target-frequency impedance and return loss, bandwidth, efficiency, gain, electrical mesh size, power balance, agreement between model fidelities and omitted physical effects. Designs containing a substrate are re-evaluated by the analytical model with unit relative permittivity so that the reported discrepancy isolates model-form error from the absent dielectric layer.
  2. Converge. A second solve on a 0.7× mesh reports how far the resonance and |Z| moved.
  3. Calibrate. The template is wrapped so its closed-form resonance and resistance are scaled to the full-wave values. Geometry, parameter bounds and optimizers are untouched, only the fast surrogate changes.
  4. Iteration. Optimization, verification and recalibration are repeated while a low-cost connectivity test penalizes feed or shorting pins that fail to intersect a conductor. This constraint was introduced after the analytical objective accepted a planar inverted-F antenna with a feed outside the patch, which the full-wave model correctly represented as an open circuit.

Five optimization and verification cycles for an air-loaded planar inverted-F antenna at 2.45 GHz showed surrogate resonance errors ranging from -44 to 17 percent across candidate geometries. The variation excluded correction by a single global scale factor and supported full-wave refinement of the highest-ranked candidate designs.

10. Electromagnetic response in lossy tissue

Far-field gain and radiation efficiency were omitted for the unbounded lossy-medium calculation because radiated power requires specification of a finite integration boundary, whereas input impedance remains well defined within the homogeneous-medium formulation.

11. Software integration

The full-wave solver implements the analytical solver interface used by the optimization objective and is available through the simulate_fullwave, verify_fullwave and fidelity_ladder agent tools, a command-line interface and the Streamlit application. Each interface reports impedance and return-loss comparisons, agreement grades, numerical diagnostics, surface-current distributions and three-dimensional gain patterns, with Gmsh initialization configured to avoid installation of signal handlers inside the Streamlit worker thread.

12. Model limitations

Homogeneous-medium approximation. The present formulation represents conductors in one homogeneous medium and therefore omits explicit dielectric interfaces. Reports estimate the expected resonance displacement using \(1-1/\sqrt{\varepsilon_{r,eff}}\), which may remain limited for electrically thin substrates but becomes substantial for patch antennas on FR-4 and motivates implementation of layered-medium Green functions.
  • Thin sheets only, thick blocks are meshed as closed shells, and closed shells carry EFIE interior resonances at discrete frequencies (a combined-field formulation would remove them).
  • Oblique 3D wires (the helix template) are refused with a message, a wire-kernel solver is the right tool there.
  • Dense O(N²) storage, about 8,000 unknowns is the practical ceiling on a laptop.
  • In a lossy medium only the input impedance is produced.

13. Planned extensions

  • Layered-medium Green function. Spectral-domain evaluation with discrete complex images would represent substrate interfaces and stratified skin, fat and muscle, enabling direct full-wave optimization of implant geometries.
  • Two-antenna links. The multi-port path already works, an implant and an external reader in one impedance matrix gives \(S_{21}\) directly, a physics-based link budget instead of Friis with assumed gains.
  • Full-wave in the loop on the optimizer's top candidates, now that the ladder has shown the surrogate's error is not a constant.
  • A compiled kernel (Numba or C++) for the fill, which is embarrassingly parallel and would push the ceiling past 20,000 unknowns.
  • Chaining into measurement. The pipeline already calibrates simulation against VNA data, the ladder should end at the bench, full-wave → measured S1P → corrected model.

14. Conclusions

The principal implementation risk was not the established EFIE formulation but the capacity of numerical and geometric errors to produce plausible resonances, impedance curves and efficiencies. Independent invariants including power conservation, reciprocity, Mie-series agreement and mesh convergence, together with experiments that varied one numerical component at a time, were required to distinguish physical behaviour from implementation artifacts and now form the verification basis of the solver.

title: Viability-guided policy optimization for step-level credit assignment
desc: Step-level reinforcement learning with an exact reachability oracle improved policy-only Pass@1 over supervised fine-tuning and IPO, while oracle-guided reranking achieved 0.884 Pass@1 using 33-fold fewer generated training tokens than RLOO.
heroCaption: Distribution of solution-preserving transitions and failure of greedy target-proximity heuristics across random Countdown instances.
body:
Sandra Yang and Kun Hyung Roh / Stanford University / Qwen2.5-0.5B / Countdown / one NVIDIA H100 on Modal / model checkpoint

Sequential reasoning models frequently generate locally valid operations that irreversibly remove every path to a correct solution, while terminal rewards provide no direct evidence about the transition responsible for failure. We developed viability-guided policy optimization, which assigns step-level reward according to exact reachability of the target state, and evaluated its theoretical credit-assignment properties, training efficiency, predictive performance and characteristic failure modes on Countdown arithmetic.

1. Failure localization in sequential arithmetic reasoning

Countdown requires a model to combine a finite set of numbers with addition, subtraction, multiplication and division until the target value is obtained, using each number once. Because every operation replaces two values with their result, arithmetically valid transitions can be divided into viable moves that preserve at least one solution and irreversible moves that render the target unreachable, even when both appear locally plausible from the numerical distance to the target.

Supervised fine-tuning observes one demonstrated trajectory, direct preference optimization and identity preference optimization compare complete responses and reinforcement learning with leave-one-out baselines assigns verifier reward to the terminal answer. Each approach therefore distributes learning signal across the full trace, leaving the optimization procedure to infer which earlier transition eliminated the remaining solution set.

2. Viability-guided policy optimization

The finite Countdown state graph permits exact computation of whether a target remains reachable from any intermediate state, allowing the residual solution horizon to be defined by dynamic programming over canonical multisets of rational numbers.

\[ d_y(s)=\begin{cases}0 & s\ni y\\ 1+\min_{a\in\mathcal A(s)} d_y(T(s,a)) & |s|>1\\ \infty & |s|=1,\ s\not\ni y\end{cases}\qquad \mathrm{Alive}_y(s)=\mathbf 1[d_y(s)<\infty]. \]

An action receives a viability label from the reachability of its successor state and a reward of 1 for a viable transition, 0.1 for a legal but irreversible transition and 0 for an unparsable or arithmetically invalid output. Exact rational arithmetic removes ambiguity from division, while memoization reduces the cost of oracle evaluation because a typical solvable four-number instance contains approximately twenty viable states.

Training uses self-play with a group-relative policy gradient in which the policy samples eight candidate transitions at each state, the oracle assigns viability rewards and a leave-one-out advantage weights the log probability of each sampled action.

\[ \mathcal L(\theta)=-\frac1G\sum_{i=1}^G A_i\log\pi_\theta(\hat a_i\mid p(s,h))+\lambda_{\mathrm{KL}}\widehat{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})-\lambda_{\mathrm{ent}}\widehat H(\pi_\theta). \]

The optimization objective retains the group-relative form of RLOO while replacing terminal verification with a transition-level reachability signal. Rollouts advance through a sampled viable action, with an oracle-supplied viable transition used during early training only when the policy produces none, thereby exposing the model to later reasoning states without using the oracle during policy-only evaluation.

3. Theoretical properties

Exact reachability labels support formal guarantees for action validity, convergence under viability-preserving policies and the sample complexity separating transition supervision from terminal reward.

  • Soundness and completeness. The label \(z_y(s,a)=1\) holds if and only if at least one legal continuation from the successor state reaches the target, making the continuation a constructive witness of viability.
  • Convergence under viable actions. From a viable initial state, a deterministic policy that selects a viable action at every nonterminal state reaches the target within at most \(m-1\) transitions because each operation reduces the multiset cardinality by one and preserves reachability. A transition to a nonviable state is consequently irreversible.
  • Exponential separation in credit assignment. In a depth-\(H\) search tree with branching factor \(B\), one viable action at each depth and terminal-only reward, identifying a viable root action through random continuation requires \(N=\Omega\!\left(B^{H-1}\log(1/\delta)\right)\) samples to observe a success with probability \(1-\delta\). One exact reachability query determines the same label because the random-continuation probability is \(p=B^{-(H-1)}\) and \((1-p)^N\le\delta\) implies \(N\ge\log(1/\delta)/(-\log(1-p))=\Theta(p^{-1}\log(1/\delta))\).

4. Experimental design and computational budget

All methods were initialized from the same Qwen2.5-0.5B model fine-tuned on Countdown demonstrations and evaluated by an identical rule-based scorer that assigned 1.0 to a valid equation using every number once, 0.1 to a well-formed but incorrect expression and 0 to an unparsable response. Viability-guided optimization used 200 self-play updates on one H100 with batches of eight states, eight candidates per state, a learning rate of 10-5, KL and entropy coefficients of 10-3 and a sampling temperature of 0.8, followed by evaluation on 500 held-out problems with 16 rollouts per prompt and 95 percent Wilson intervals.

The trained checkpoint was evaluated as VPO-A, which selected the first legal candidate without oracle access, and as VPO-R, which used the reachability oracle to select a viable candidate from the same sampled set. VPO-A measures the policy acquired during training, whereas VPO-R estimates the performance attainable when viability information is retained during inference.

Computational efficiency was evaluated using both the number of reward evaluations and the number of generated training tokens because transition and terminal supervision operate at different sequence lengths. RLOO used approximately 102,400 verifier evaluations and 50.7 million generated tokens, compared with approximately 64,000 oracle evaluations and 1.54 million generated tokens for viability-guided optimization.

5. Results

Policy-only VPO-A achieved lower Pass@1 than RLOO, with estimates of 0.486 and 0.618, respectively, showing that the largest improvement arose from reachability-based reranking during inference. A single reranked VPO-R response achieved Pass@1 of 0.884, which was comparable to the supervised seed's Pass@16 of 0.888 and indicates that viability filtering compressed much of the benefit of sixteen independent samples into one selected response.

5.1 Training dynamics

6. Ablation analysis

Aggressive repair changes the group sampling distribution at the point where the leave-one-out advantage is calculated by introducing actions not generated by the current policy. As the viable-action rate increases, infrequent replacements can therefore assign gradients to off-policy tokens with uncorrected importance ratios, providing a plausible mechanism for the late optimization instability observed in the ablation.

7. Prevalence of irreversible transitions in Countdown

The prevalence of irreversible legal transitions was quantified using an independently implemented exact rational dynamic program applied to 3,000 uniformly sampled four-number instances with operands and targets between 1 and 99.

The failure of the numerically closest transition in 53 percent of sampled instances shows that immediate proximity to the target is poorly aligned with preservation of the global solution set, despite its plausibility as a heuristic learned from successful demonstrations. Representative instances with their greedy and viable transitions are shown below.

numbers → targetgreedy move (closest to target)alive moves instead
[2, 8, 12, 71] → 938 × 12 = 96 · dead2 + 8, 2 + 12, 2 + 71, 8 + 12 …
[19, 29, 31, 70] → 5829 + 31 = 60 · dead31 − 19 = 12, 19 + 70 = 89 …
[25, 32, 43, 81] → 381 ÷ 25 · dead32 + 43 = 75 (the only one)

These prevalence estimates describe a uniform distribution over operands and targets rather than the solvable-instance distribution used for model training, but they establish that irreversible legal transitions are common across the state space and therefore provide a frequent source of credit-assignment ambiguity.

7.1 Interactive viability analysis

The interactive implementation applies the same exact dynamic program used to construct the training reward, labels every legal transition according to successor-state reachability and reports the residual solution horizon after each selected action.

viability oracle

8. Implementation

The oracle in countdown_oracle.py computes the minimum solution horizon, state viability and transition labels over canonical rational multisets, while countdown_step_env.py parses generated operations, verifies arithmetic and operand use and records viability and residual-distance metadata. Training alternates between vLLM sampling and grouped PyTorch optimization through on-disk checkpoints because the workers cannot occupy the GPU simultaneously, with KL divergence and entropy estimated from sampled tokens and loss restricted to generated transition tokens.

Comparator implementations were developed and validated before the viability experiments, with IPO trained for one epoch on 48,000 preference pairs using \(\beta=0.05\) and RLOO trained for 100 updates of 128 prompts with eight rollouts and a clipped sequence-level importance weight. Both methods were evaluated on the milestone test set before inclusion in the final comparison.

9. Limitations

  • Viability-guided optimization and RLOO receive rewards at different temporal resolutions, requiring computational comparison through both reward evaluations and generated tokens rather than a single feedback count.
  • VPO-R retains oracle access during inference and therefore estimates performance with reachability-guided selection, whereas policy-only VPO-A provides the direct comparison with supervised fine-tuning and IPO and remains below RLOO on Pass@1.
  • Exact reachability is available for Countdown, while extension to domains that require simulation, constraint solving or a learned critic will depend on the calibration and error structure of the approximate viability estimator.
  • The experiments use a 0.5-billion-parameter model and a finite arithmetic task, leaving the behaviour of viability supervision at larger model and state-space scales unresolved.

10. Future directions

  • Approximate viability estimation. A learned value model trained from exact oracle labels could quantify how reachability error affects policy optimization and establish operating thresholds for tasks without an exact state predicate.
  • Policy distillation. Supervision from oracle-selected candidates could transfer the inference-time advantage of VPO-R into the policy and test whether the observed Pass@1 difference can be recovered without oracle access.
  • Higher-dimensional state spaces. Sokoban-style planning and type-constrained program synthesis provide larger search graphs in which locally valid actions can irreversibly eliminate the goal while partial viability checks remain computationally accessible.
  • Mechanistic analysis of repair instability. Logging the importance ratios and gradient contributions of inserted teacher actions would test whether off-policy contamination explains the observed late-stage collapse.

title: Molecular age prediction through multimodal integration and few-shot learning
desc: Evaluation of DNA-methylation and microbial age predictors, residual multimodal integration and few-shot adaptation across external cohorts.
heroCaption: Participant-held-out evaluation of microbial integration, repeated-validation stability and source-study heterogeneity.
body:
Iteration 1 / Blood methylation and microbiomeIteration 2 / Few-shot adaptation

Iteration 1Blood methylation and microbiome integration

Abstract

Age-associated molecular variation is distributed across host epigenetic and microbial measurements, but multimodal prediction is constrained by cohort structure and incomplete specimen pairing. We evaluated DNA-methylation and skin-microbiome age predictors in public cohorts comprising 360 discovery blood samples, 274 external blood samples and 1,798 skin samples from 339 participant identifiers. Plate-held-out validation of the methylation model yielded a mean absolute error (MAE) of 4.21 years, participant-held-out validation of the skin-microbiome model yielded an MAE of 9.17 years. External methylation validation yielded an MAE of 6.03 years, indicating reduced transportability across study populations.

Within the skin cohort, residual integration of microbial features with study, body site and sex reduced participant-weighted MAE from 9.71 to 8.74 years, corresponding to a paired reduction of 0.97 years (95% conditional bootstrap interval, 0.66–1.28). In a separate paired cohort of 123 participants, early integration of a methylation-clock score with gut microbial features degraded performance, whereas a clock-preserving residual formulation recovered clock-level accuracy (MAE, 4.85 years) without a detectable improvement over methylation calibration alone. These analyses demonstrate context-dependent microbial information while identifying specimen pairing, study heterogeneity and preservation of strong unimodal predictors as central constraints on multimodal age prediction.

Results

Cohort composition and prediction architecture

Microbial features improve age prediction conditional on cohort metadata

Joint modelling of microbial features and cohort metadata achieved a participant-weighted mean absolute error of 8.74 years, compared with 9.71 years for metadata alone and 9.15 years for microbial features alone. The reductions of 0.97 years relative to metadata and 0.41 years relative to microbial features had 95% conditional intervals of 0.66 to 1.28 years and 0.10 to 0.74 years, respectively.

Although the pooled improvement was recovered in each validation repetition, estimates within individual studies ranged from a 1.53-year reduction in study 10317 to a 0.46-year increase in study 1841, with study 2010 showing a 0.19-year reduction. Study 10317 contributed 237 of the 339 participant identifiers and accounted for most of the aggregate effect, indicating that the predictive contribution of microbial features varied with cohort composition.

Early integration degrades prediction in a paired methylation-clock and gut-microbiome cohort

The paired analysis used the HI-SEED release, comprising 123 participants with concordant identifiers across metadata and microbial abundance tables. Across three repeated five-fold validations, calibrated Horvath scores achieved an MAE of 4.87 years, genus-level microbial profiles achieved 12.59 years and early feature integration achieved 9.53 years. Relative to calibrated methylation scores, integration increased MAE by 4.66 years (95% conditional interval, 3.35–6.03). The analysis uses a pretrained methylation-clock score rather than raw methylation measurements and has not been externally validated.

Clock-preserving residual integration recovers unimodal predictive accuracy

A subsequent formulation retained an unpenalized clock-calibration term and estimated an independent correction from clock-orthogonalized microbial features. Across identical outer partitions, residual integration achieved an MAE of 4.848 years, compared with 4.851 years for inner-selected clock calibration and 4.870 years for ordinary least-squares calibration. Relative to early feature integration (MAE, 9.529 years), the post hoc paired reduction was 4.68 years (95% conditional interval, 3.42–6.07), equivalent to a 49.1% reduction.

Comparison with inner-selected clock calibration yielded a mean reduction of 0.004 years with a 95% conditional interval from -0.061 to 0.070 years, despite selection of a microbial correction in 12 of 15 outer training partitions. Residual integration consequently recovered the predictive accuracy lost through early concatenation, while providing no measurable evidence that genus-level microbial features improved prediction beyond methylation-score calibration.

Plate-held-out validation of the blood methylation model yielded an R² of 0.91, whereas evaluation in an external cohort of control women aged 52 to 78 years yielded a mean absolute error of 6.03 years and an R² of -1.38. The decline in external performance, including a squared error greater than that obtained from the external cohort mean, indicates substantial sensitivity to differences between the discovery and validation populations.

Participant-held-out prediction from skin microbial composition yielded a mean absolute error of 9.17 years, compared with 10.06 years for a model containing study, body site and sex, which corresponded to a paired reduction of 0.89 years with a 95% conditional interval of 0.46 to 1.32 years. Microbial composition therefore captured age-associated variation beyond the recorded cohort variables, while the performance of the metadata model showed that study design and sampling site explained a substantial proportion of the predictive signal.

Sampling structure and external validity

Random sample partitioning placed observations from previously encountered participants in 90.5% of the test samples, whereas participant-level and study-level partitioning removed this overlap. Under participant holdout, the participant-weighted mean absolute error increased from 8.93 to 9.24 years, with a paired increase of 0.31 years and a 95% conditional interval of 0.15 to 0.48 years, while sample weighting reduced the apparent error for the same predictions to 6.44 years and demonstrated the influence of repeated sampling on performance estimates.

Generalization across studies was markedly weaker than performance within participant-held-out partitions, with leave-one-study-out validation yielding a mean absolute error of 18.35 years. Study 1841 consisted predominantly of younger adults, whereas study 10317 spanned a broader and older population, suggesting that differences in age distribution and study-specific measurement structure contributed to the loss of predictive accuracy.

Assay quality and feature interpretation

Two samples in the external blood cohort exceeded 1% missing CpG measurements, including one sample with approximately 57% missingness whose predicted age was -28.4 years at a recorded age of 74 years. Applying a 1% missingness threshold to the recorded predictions retained 272 controls and changed the mean absolute error to 5.48 years and the R² to -0.26, indicating that assay completeness contributed materially to the external error distribution.

CpGs annotated to NHLRC1, SCGN and ASPA were selected in all five outer training sets and carried among the largest standardized coefficients in the methylation model, while the highest microbial importance ranks included amplicon sequence variants assigned to Mycoplasma and Enterobacteriaceae. These model-derived rankings identify reproducible predictive features whose biological interpretation remains dependent on correlated measurements, study effects and the taxonomic resolution of the released data.

Across both molecular modalities, models fitted to the observed age labels produced lower mean absolute error than each of ten matched label-permutation runs, providing evidence that the selected feature matrices contained learnable age-associated structure while leaving the magnitude of permutation-based significance imprecisely estimated.

Probe-aware pathway analysis identifies no FDR-significant enrichment

The 500 methylation probes selected by the final model mapped to 472 unique genes, which were evaluated across 1,333 Reactome pathways using the 14,475 genes represented on the array as the measured background. None of the tested pathways passed Benjamini-Hochberg correction at a false discovery rate below 0.05, and the nominally ranked pathways shown in Figure 3 are consequently interpreted as hypotheses for biological investigation rather than evidence of pathway-level enrichment.

Discussion

Repeated participant-held-out validation showed that skin microbial features improved chronological age prediction beyond study, body site and sex, with a consistent pooled reduction in error across three partition seeds. The concentration of this improvement in the largest source study, together with the marked deterioration under study-level holdout, indicates that the microbial signal included both age-associated information shared across participants and structure specific to the contributing cohorts.

Analysis of the paired HI-SEED cohort showed that the effect of multimodal integration depended strongly on the statistical formulation, because direct concatenation of methylation-clock scores and microbial abundances degraded prediction whereas residual integration preserved the accuracy of the calibrated methylation score. The microbial correction did not improve performance beyond calibration alone, suggesting that the available genus-level measurements did not provide stable complementary information after the methylation-derived age estimate had been modelled.

For component errors eb and es, fusion error variance satisfies,

Var(efusion) = w² Var(eb) + (1 − w)² Var(es) + 2w(1 − w) Cov(eb, es).

Because the blood methylation and skin microbiome measurements were obtained from different individuals, the covariance and joint bias of the two component errors could not be estimated from these cohorts. A definitive evaluation of blood and skin integration will require paired specimens collected from the same participants, estimation of fusion parameters within training or calibration data and comparison with both unimodal predictors in an independent test cohort.

The interpretation of these findings is further constrained by reliance on processed public matrices, ambiguous participant identifiers in one excluded microbiome study, restricted age coverage in the external methylation cohort and residual assay and study effects. Chronological age was the sole prediction target, and associations with physiological ageing, disease susceptibility or clinical outcomes remain to be determined in appropriately designed cohorts.

Methods

Clock-preserving residual models

Within each training partition, clock calibration was selected among ordinary least squares, Huber regression and unpenalized median regression, after which Hellinger-transformed microbial features were orthogonalized with respect to the clock by multivariate linear regression fitted exclusively to the training data. Linear and radial basis function kernel ridge models predicted residual age after clock calibration, with three-fold inner validation selecting the calibration model, kernel, regularization parameter and correction magnitude inside each of three five-fold participant partitions. Conditional intervals were obtained by resampling participant-level losses averaged across repetitions, and the complete model comparison is reported in the model summary.

Paired clock-score pilot

Within each training fold, Horvath scores were calibrated by linear regression and genus abundances were transformed by the sample-local Hellinger procedure before standardization of the microbiome and concatenated clock-microbiome feature matrices. Three-fold inner validation selected ridge regularization from values of 0.1, 1, 10, 100 and 1,000 within each of three seeded five-fold participant partitions, while clinical outcomes, age-acceleration residuals and the ambiguously scaled GrimAge2 column were excluded from the predictors. Conditional intervals were calculated from 10,000 resamples of participant-level losses averaged across repetitions.

Datasets and eligibility criteria

Blood methylation data from GSE41037 supplied 360 discovery samples after restriction of 720 deposited specimens to healthy adults with a positive source quality-control flag, while 274 control women from GSE19711 formed the external validation cohort. Both processed matrices contained 27,578 CpG identifiers, and age at recruitment was used as the external outcome because the precise age at blood collection was unavailable.

Skin microbial abundances and metadata were obtained from the Huang et al. repository. The released matrix contained 1,975 samples and 7,311 amplicon sequence variants (ASVs). Study 11052 was excluded because all 177 samples shared one participant identifier despite discrepant age values. The retained dataset comprised 1,798 samples and 339 study-qualified participant identifiers across three studies. Thirteen retained identifiers had one-year differences in recorded age across samples, all samples associated with an identifier remained in the same validation fold.

Skin observations were weighted inversely by the number of samples per participant during fitting and primary evaluation. This prevented participants with repeated sampling from contributing disproportionate weight. Dataset composition and age distributions are reported in Figure 1. The source microbial matrix had undergone age-independent prevalence filtering before release, that upstream processing could not be reconstructed from the available table.

Modality-specific age prediction

The methylation pipeline comprised median imputation, age-correlation feature selection, standardization, and ridge regression. Five outer folds held out complete assay plates. Three-fold plate-grouped inner validation selected 100 or 500 CpGs and ridge regularization parameters α ∈ {10, 100, 1000}. Every preprocessing operation was fitted within the relevant training partition. A final discovery-only selection identified 500 CpGs and α = 100, the resulting model was applied to the external controls without age-based recalibration.

The microbiome pipeline applied a sample-local Hellinger transformation, equivalent to the square root of relative abundance, and a training-only prevalence threshold of 1%. Random forests contained 160 trees with square-root feature subsampling. Minimum leaf sizes of 1, 3, and 5 were compared using three-fold participant-grouped inner validation within five outer participant-grouped folds. A minimum leaf size of 1 was selected in every outer fold and used for the final component refit. Final refitting does not provide an additional estimate of prediction accuracy.

Late-fusion architecture

The integrated estimator combines the component predictions for a shared participant,

ŷfusion = w ŷblood + (1 − w) ŷskin,   w = 0.5.

The prediction-level integration model assigns equal weight to methylation and microbiome estimates for participants with verified specimen linkage, while preserving separate modality-specific inference when only one assay is available. The implementation requires concordant participant indices and fitted feature schemas and rejects missing, duplicated or discordant identifiers, thereby preventing construction of artificial pairs from age or row order.

The fitted model artifact contains both modality-specific regressors, their feature identifiers and the equal-weight fusion operator, with training performed on four Modal CPU cores and serialization verified by reproducing the recorded predictions. Refitting changed the external blood predictions by no more than 0.00014 years across compute environments, while evaluation of the joint output was deferred because verified paired blood and skin specimens were unavailable.

Validation and statistical analysis

Validation included training-age median baselines for both modalities and a skin metadata ridge model containing study, body site and sex, together with a fixed random forest evaluated under random-sample, participant-held-out and leave-one-study-out partitions. Ten matched label-permutation runs were performed for each modality, with skin labels permuted at the level of participant-mean age to preserve the repeated-sampling structure.

Mean absolute error, root mean squared error and R² were calculated from held-out predictions, with uncertainty estimated from 2,000 bootstrap resamples of assay plates for internal blood validation, samples for external blood validation and participants for skin validation. Analyses used random seed 20260905, and comparisons between modalities were interpreted with respect to the demographic composition and age range of their distinct source cohorts.

Repeated evaluation of microbiome–metadata integration

An exploratory follow-up evaluated whether microbial features improve prediction beyond study, body site, and sex. The experiment specification and source-code hash were recorded before execution. All three specified seeds (20260906, 20260907, and 20260908), all comparisons, and all source studies were retained. Because the cohorts had already been analyzed, this is a follow-up analysis rather than independent external confirmation.

The combined estimator added predictions from a metadata ridge model with a regularization parameter of 10 to predictions from a 160-tree random forest fitted to microbial residuals, with one-hot encoding, prevalence filtering and residual construction repeated within every training partition. Inner validation selected microbial forest leaf sizes of 1, 3 or 8 and compared the metadata ridge model with a metadata forest, while a separately tuned microbial forest provided the secondary comparator.

Each repetition used five outer participant-grouped folds and three inner participant-grouped folds. The primary endpoint was the participant-weighted MAE reduction versus the inner-selected metadata model, reduction versus microbial prediction alone was secondary. Absolute errors were averaged within participant across repeated samples and the three repetitions. Conditional intervals used 10,000 paired participant bootstrap resamples stratified by source study. This analysis measures predictive information within the sampled study mixture and does not establish transfer to an unseen study.

Iteration 2Few-shot adaptation across methylation cohorts

To determine whether epigenetic age predictors can be adapted when few labelled samples are available from a new cohort, we evaluated episodic representation learning and support-conditioned regression across two independent blood-derived methylation datasets.

Abstract

Epigenetic age predictors are sensitive to population composition, blood-cell source and assay design, yet target-domain labels are often scarce. We evaluated a neural representation trained by episodic optimization and adapted by differentiable ridge regression in two independent methylation cohorts. The source analysis comprised 542 training samples and 92 samples reserved for checkpoint selection, external evaluation comprised 588 query participants separated from support pools of 8, 16 or 32 labelled individuals. At 16 labels, the augmented model achieved mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 7.293 years in whole blood and 3.670 years in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), compared with 7.620 and 4.053 years for support-selected classical comparators. The corresponding paired MAE reductions were 0.326 years (95% conditional interval, 0.185–0.472, Holm-adjusted P = 0.0002) and 0.384 years (0.211–0.573, P = 0.0002). A frozen source ridge model retained lower error in whole blood, and affine recalibration was statistically indistinguishable from the neural adapter in PBMCs. These results identify a reproducible advantage over support-set model selection while delimiting the conditions under which few-shot adaptation improves upon fixed or assay-matched source models.

Results

Source-domain learning and independent external evaluation

Healthy adult control samples from GSE41037 and control women from GSE19711 provided 634 source samples. Discovery plate H (92 samples) was reserved for source-only checkpoint selection, the remaining 542 samples supplied feature selection, preprocessing, source-clock fitting and neural training. The model used 1,024 CpGs selected exclusively in the source-training partition. The external whole-blood cohort GSE40279 contained 656 participants aged 19–101 years. The PBMC release GSE37008 contained 99 deposited arrays, 92 participants aged 24–45 years remained after the specified quality filters and identifier audit.

Fixed random support pools contained 128 whole-blood participants and 32 PBMC participants, leaving 528 and 60 query participants. Query participants never entered model fitting, support-only baseline selection or checkpoint selection. Twenty seeded support draws were evaluated at each label budget, with the 16-shot comparison specified as primary. The target releases contained observations for 834 and 809 of the 1,024 selected probes, entirely unavailable probes were imputed using source-training medians.

Few-shot adaptation improves upon support-selected comparators

At the prespecified 16-label endpoint, neural adaptation reduced mean absolute error by 4.3% in whole blood and 9.5% in peripheral blood mononuclear cells relative to the classical comparator selected within each support set, with both paired contrasts remaining significant after Holm correction across cohorts. The effects were estimated across the recorded support draws and external query participants, establishing a consistent advantage over data-limited model selection within these two target cohorts.

The improvement in whole blood was greatest with eight labelled participants and diminished as the support set increased, whereas predictions in peripheral blood mononuclear cells remained close to affine recalibration across label budgets. Comparison of all estimators at 16 labels showed that the neural model primarily improved the reliability of adaptation selected from very small support sets rather than uniformly surpassing every fixed estimator.

Performance relative to fixed classical estimators

In whole blood, the frozen source ridge model achieved a mean absolute error of 6.842 years, compared with 7.293 years for the augmented neural model and 7.038 and 7.052 years for linear and radial basis function residual kernels. In peripheral blood mononuclear cells, affine recalibration achieved an error of 3.854 years, and its 0.185-year difference from the neural adapter had a conditional interval that included zero, indicating that the significant primary contrasts arose from improved performance relative to support-selected comparators rather than superiority over every individual estimator.

Augmentation and assay-availability diagnostics

Removing synthetic feature augmentation yielded mean absolute errors of 7.266 years in whole blood and 3.656 years in peripheral blood mononuclear cells, which were marginally lower than the corresponding augmented estimates. The evaluated perturbation distribution therefore did not improve prediction, while variation in source-validation performance across training checkpoints supported the use of data independent from episodic optimization for checkpoint selection.

Refitting the source ridge model with probes represented in each target assay produced mean absolute errors of 6.094 years in whole blood and 7.893 years in peripheral blood mononuclear cells, whereas offset-only calibration produced errors of 7.088 and 4.020 years. These opposing cohort-specific responses indicate that neither unavailable probes nor a shift in mean calibration was sufficient to explain the observed transport error.

Discussion

Episodic neural adaptation reduced prediction error relative to support-selected classical comparators in two external methylation cohorts, demonstrating that a representation learned in the source domain can improve model selection when target labels are scarce. The frozen source predictor nevertheless remained strongest in whole blood, while neural adaptation performed similarly to affine recalibration in peripheral blood mononuclear cells, showing that the value of adaptation depended on tissue composition and assay context.

Further development should model the expected benefit of adaptation as a function of assay coverage, tissue composition and molecular divergence between source and target cohorts, since these factors produced distinct responses to probe matching and calibration. Validation in additional cohorts will be required to determine whether the observed improvements extend beyond GSE40279 and GSE37008 and to define the settings in which limited target supervision provides a reproducible advantage.

Methods

Preprocessing and source prediction

Normalized M-values reported for GSE37008 were converted to beta values using β = 1/(1 + 2−M) before application of source-derived scaling, as required by the measurement definition in the sample table. Scale auditing identified and replaced an initial evaluation performed directly on M-values while retaining the model weights, hyperparameter grid and support and query partitions, and every reported peripheral blood mononuclear cell result derives from the corrected beta-value analysis.

Missing measurements were imputed with source-training medians before age-correlation screening selected 1,024 CpGs, after which values were standardized within the source data and clipped at eight standard deviations. Group-held-out validation selected the source ridge regularization parameter from values of 10, 100 and 1,000, and group out-of-fold clock predictions supplied the residual targets used during episodic neural training. Feature selection preceded the internal regularization comparison, whereas all external query comparisons remained isolated from this source-domain development procedure.

Differentiable few-shot adaptation

The encoder comprised linear layers of dimensions 1,024 → 128 → 32 with LayerNorm, GELU and tanh. Its output was concatenated with a learned scaling of the source-clock prediction. For support embeddings H and source-clock residuals r, centered kernel ridge regression fitted a residual correction with a learned positive regularization parameter. The query prediction was the source-clock estimate plus the support-fitted residual intercept and kernel correction. Gradients through the linear solve trained the encoder, regularization and clock-coordinate scale.

Six T4 GPU runs each used 2,000 source-domain episodes optimized with AdamW, comprising three random seeds for each augmentation condition and disjoint support and query samples within every episode. Task-level Gaussian shifts, multiplicative scales and feature masking were applied to encoder inputs while source-clock values remained fixed, and twelve 16-shot episodes from the source-validation plate selected checkpoints at intervals of 100 training steps before predictions were ensembled across seeds.

Classical comparators and statistical analysis

The baseline family comprised unchanged source ridge, support median, affine recalibration, target-only ridge, linear residual kernel adaptation and RBF residual kernel adaptation. Kernel regularization used α ∈ {0.01, 0.1, 1, 10}, four-fold cross-validation within each support set selected hyperparameters and the primary classical comparator. All methods used identical support/query partitions and source-selected input features. The fixed external query labels were accessed only for evaluation.

For each query participant, absolute errors were averaged over 20 support draws. Ten thousand paired participant bootstrap samples supplied conditional intervals, conditional two-sided sign-flip tests supplied P values. Sign-flip inference assumes exchangeability of signed paired losses. Holm correction covered the two primary cohort contrasts, with secondary contrasts corrected as a separate exploratory family. Shared support pools, source-model retraining uncertainty and uncertainty from selecting the fixed support pool are not captured by these intervals. At 32 shots in PBMCs, the complete 32-person pool is reused, only support-CV assignments vary. Two external cohorts do not establish general population-wide validity.
